title: Concrete mix design: why the water–cement ratio sets the strength
examples: Why does the water–cement ratio matter?
How do you design a concrete mix?
What is the target strength for M25 concrete?

marks.label: w/c = 0.50
marks.ask: Why does more water make concrete weaker?

explain.say: In nineteen eighteen Duff Abrams, testing concrete in Chicago, found one rule that still governs every mix: the less water for each kilo of cement, the stronger the concrete. On the board, strength falls steadily as the water–cement ratio rises. Let us see why, and then use it to design a mix.

explain.say: Read the curve at a ratio of zero point five: about thirty seven megapascals. Add water to make it zero point seven, a soupy mix that is easy to pour, and strength drops to about twenty one. Why? The extra water does not react; it evaporates and leaves tiny pores, like holes in a sponge. Which mix would you choose for a bridge pier?

explain.say: The low ratio one! Here is a typical recipe for one cubic metre: three hundred and fifty kilos of cement, one hundred and seventy five of water, seven hundred of sand and eleven hundred and fifty of gravel. The water–cement ratio is one seventy five over three fifty, zero point five. See how sand and stone make up most of it?

Mix design runs in steps. First set a target above the grade, because real batches vary. For grade M25 with a standard deviation of four, the target is twenty five plus one point six five times four, thirty one point six megapascals. Then pick the water–cement ratio from a curve like ours, and the water needed for the workability you want.

Last, make a trial batch and crush test cubes. Too stiff to place? Never add water on site; add a plasticiser, a chemical that makes the mix flow without weakening it. Well done! Challenge: a mix has four hundred kilos of cement and one hundred and sixty of water. What is its ratio, and is it stronger than our recipe?

marks.label: w/c = 0.50
marks.ask: Why does more water make concrete weaker?

faq.a: It is the mass of water divided by the mass of cement in a mix. One hundred and seventy five kilos of water with three hundred and fifty of cement gives 0.5.

faq.q: Why does more water make concrete weaker?
faq.a: Cement needs only part of the water to react. The rest evaporates and leaves pores, so the hardened paste is weaker and lets in water and chemicals more easily.
asks: Why does a wet mix lose strength?

faq.a: It is the average strength a mix is designed for, set above the grade so almost all batches pass. India's IS 10262 uses f_ck plus 1.65 times the standard deviation, so 31.6 megapascals for M25 with s equal to 4.
Workability is how easily fresh concrete can be placed and compacted. The slump test measures it: a cone of concrete is lifted and the drop in height is the slump, in millimetres.
A plasticiser, or water reducer, is a chemical admixture that makes concrete flow more easily, so the same workability needs less water and the concrete is stronger.

facts: Duff Abrams published the water–cement ratio law in 1918.
India's IS 10262:2019 sets target mean strength as f_ck + 1.65 s.
Normal-weight concrete has a density of about 2400 kilograms per cubic metre.
